title: RSIFlow: Adaptive Self-Improvement Workflows with an Evolving Meta-Agent
title_zh: RSIFlow: 基于进化元智能体的自适应自我改进工作流

paragraphs.en: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in complex tasks, including code generation, tool use, and multi-hop question answering. Existing self-improvement methods enhance agent performance through model optimization, harness evolution, and executable artifact refinement, while recursive self-improvement (RSI) further extends optimization to the improvement mechanisms themselves. However, adapting self-improvement workflows to evolving performance bottlenecks while improving workflow orchestration through execution feedback remains a key challenge. We propose RSIFlow , a R ecursive S elf- I mprovement framework that integrates adaptive work flow orchestration with meta-agent capability evolution. RSIFlow diagnoses performance bottlenecks from task-agent trajectories and environmental feedback to dynamically select component-specific improvement workflows. The meta-agent then distills workflow outcomes into component-specific skills and cross-component principles, evolving its own harness to improve subsequent workflow orchestration. Experiments across six benchmarks and two backbone models show that RSIFlow achieves the SOTA average performance on all benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate the contributions of adaptive workflow orchestration and meta-harness evolution. Code is available at https://github.com/1HUAN1/RSI-Flow.
paragraphs.zh: 大语言模型（LLM）智能体在复杂任务中展现出强大的能力，包括代码生成、工具使用和多跳问答。 现有的自我改进方法通过模型优化、框架演化和可执行产物精炼来提升智能体性能，而递归自我改进（RSI）进一步将优化扩展到改进机制本身。 然而，如何在通过执行反馈改进工作流编排的同时，使自我改进工作流适应不断变化的性能瓶颈，仍然是一个关键挑战。 我们提出了 RSIFlow，一个递归自我改进框架，它将自适应工作流编排与元智能体能力演化相结合。 RSIFlow 从任务-智能体轨迹和环境反馈中诊断性能瓶颈，以动态选择针对特定组件的改进工作流。 元智能体随后将工作流结果提炼为针对特定组件的技能和跨组件的原则，并演化其自身的框架以改进后续的工作流编排。 在六个基准和两个骨干模型上的实验表明，RSIFlow 在所有基准上都达到了 SOTA 的平均性能。 消融研究进一步证明了自适应工作流编排和元框架演化的贡献。 代码已发布于 https://github.com/1HUAN1/RSI-Flow。

paragraphs.en: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled agents to tackle complex tasks in coding, tool use, and multi-hop question answering ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Schick et al., 2023 ; Yao et al., 2023 ) . To continuously enhance the development of agents’ capabilities in task domains, existing methods have adopted complementary approaches, including evolving execution harnesses ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , optimizing model parameters ( Luo et al., 2025 ) , and refining executable artifacts ( Novikov et al., 2025 ) . These routes can be organized into self-improvement workflows that propose and evaluate changes using task feedback. Beyond executing such workflows, recursive self-improvement (RSI) seeks to strengthen not only task-solving capabilities but also the mechanisms that generate subsequent improvements ( Zhang et al., 2026c ; Duan et al., 2026 ) .
paragraphs.zh: 大语言模型（LLM）的最新进展使智能体能够应对编码、工具使用和多跳问答等复杂任务（ Yang et al., 2024 ; Schick et al., 2023 ; Yao et al., 2023 ）。 为了持续提升智能体在任务领域能力的发展，现有方法采用了互补的路径，包括演化执行框架（ Zhang et al., 2025 ）、优化模型参数（ Luo et al., 2025 ）以及改进可执行工件（ Novikov et al., 2025 ）。 这些路径可以组织成自我改进工作流，利用任务反馈来提出并评估变更。 除了执行此类工作流之外，递归自我改进（RSI）不仅致力于增强任务求解能力，还致力于增强生成后续改进的机制本身（ Zhang et al., 2026c ; Duan et al., 2026 ）。

paragraphs.en: Research on agent self-improvement spans three increasingly broad scopes of optimization. Component-level approaches optimize a predefined part of the system, such as the model or the harness (execution workflows) ( Luo et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) . System-level approaches coordinate updates across components, including joint model–harness optimization and feedback-driven selection of update targets ( Chen et al., 2026d ; Chen et al., 2026b ; Hebbar et al., 2026 ) . Meta-level approaches make improvement procedures editable through operator scheduling, program modification, and recursive skill evolution ( Tan et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026c ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . These developments expand both what can be modified and how modifications are organized. However, broader editability alone does not establish how effectively a workflow addresses the agent’s current bottlenecks, or whether the ability to organize that workflow improves with experience. This motivates a central question: how can RSI systems adapt self-improvement workflows to evolving bottlenecks while learning to organize these workflows more effectively?
paragraphs.zh: 关于智能体自我改进的研究涵盖了三个范围逐渐扩大的优化层面。 组件级方法优化系统中预定义的部分，例如模型或执行框架（工作流）（Luo et al., 2025；Zhang et al., 2026b）。 系统级方法协调跨组件的更新，包括模型与执行框架的联合优化，以及基于反馈选择更新目标（Chen et al., 2026d；Chen et al., 2026b；Hebbar et al., 2026）。 元级方法通过算子调度、程序修改和递归式技能演化，使改进过程本身可编辑（Tan et al., 2026；Zhang et al., 2026c；Wang et al., 2026）。 这些进展既扩展了可修改的对象范围，也扩展了修改的组织方式。 然而，仅有更广的可编辑性并不能说明某个工作流能否有效应对智能体当前的瓶颈，也不能说明组织该工作流的能力是否会随着经验积累而提升。 这引出了一个核心问题：RSI 系统如何将自我改进工作流适配到不断演化的瓶颈，同时学会更有效地组织这些工作流？

paragraphs.en: We formulate this challenge as dynamic workflow adaptation in RSI, where adapting bottlenecks and evolving workflow orchestration must be considered together. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , self-improvement workflows must adapt to bottlenecks that vary with task requirements and the agent’s capability state. Even within a fixed domain, successful updates can reshape these bottlenecks and alter the effectiveness of subsequent workflow orchestration. Meanwhile, workflow orchestration is itself a capability that can improve through experience. Feedback from workflow execution supports the accumulation and refinement of reusable knowledge for diagnosis, workflow selection, and execution. These processes form a feedback loop: task-level updates reshape improvement requirements, while workflow experience refines the orchestration capability that guides subsequent updates.
paragraphs.zh: 我们将这一挑战形式化为 RSI 中的动态工作流自适应问题，其中瓶颈的自适应与工作流编排的演化必须被放在一起考虑。 如图 1 所示，自我改进工作流必须适应随任务需求和智能体能力状态而变化的瓶颈。 即使在固定领域内，成功的更新也会重塑这些瓶颈，并改变后续工作流编排的有效性。 与此同时，工作流编排本身也是一种可以通过经验不断提升的能力。 来自工作流执行的反馈支持可复用知识的积累与精炼，这些知识用于诊断、工作流选择和执行。 这些过程构成一个反馈回路：任务级更新重塑改进需求，而工作流经验则精炼指导后续更新的编排能力。

paragraphs.en: To address this challenge, we propose RSIFlow , a framework that couples adaptive workflow orchestration with meta-agent capability evolution . We instantiate three self-improvement workflows targeting the Harness , Model , and Artifacts . A meta-agent uses execution trajectories and environmental feedback to diagnose the task agent’s bottlenecks, select a workflow, and orchestrate candidate generation and validation. It then distills orchestration outcomes into component-specific skills and cross-component principles to revise its own harness, including execution procedures and skill invocation. This experience-driven self-revision closes a recursive feedback loop in which workflow orchestration outcomes refine the orchestration mechanism that guides subsequent improvements.
paragraphs.zh: 为应对这一挑战，我们提出 RSIFlow，一个将自适应工作流编排与元智能体能力演进相结合的框架。 我们实例化了三个分别针对 Harness、Model 和 Artifacts 的自我改进工作流。 元智能体利用执行轨迹和环境反馈来诊断任务智能体的瓶颈，选择工作流，并编排候选生成与验证。 随后，它将编排结果提炼为特定组件的技能和跨组件的原则，以修订自身的 Harness，包括执行流程和技能调用。 这种经验驱动的自我修订形成了一个递归反馈回路：工作流编排的结果不断改进编排机制，而编排机制又指导后续的改进。

paragraphs.en: Many approaches to agent self-improvement optimize a single predefined component. STaR ( Zelikman et al., 2022 ) improves model parameters by repeatedly fine-tuning on self-generated rationales that yield correct answers. AFlow ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) searches code-represented workflows, while Recursive Harness Self-Improvement ( Lee et al., 2026 ) refines prompt-level harness specifications using pairwise feedback over revision histories. Related approaches include DSPy ( Khattab et al., 2024 ) for language-model pipeline optimization, GEPA ( Agrawal et al., 2026 ) for reflective prompt evolution, and ADAS ( Hu et al., 2025 ) for meta-agent-guided search over agent programs. In contrast, AlphaEvolve ( Novikov et al., 2025 ) evolves candidate programs through execution-based evaluation, targeting task artifacts rather than the agent’s improvement procedure. Self-Refine ( Madaan et al., 2023 ) iteratively revises outputs using self-feedback, while Reflexion ( Shinn et al., 2023 ) retains verbal reflections to guide subsequent attempts and Voyager ( Wang et al., 2024 ) accumulates reusable executable skills. Co-Harness ( Chen et al., 2026d ) and HarnessForge ( Chen et al., 2026b ) connect external structure and internal capability by alternating harness refinement with model optimization. Their coupled updates address model–harness compatibility, but the prescribed update order leaves open how to adapt workflow orchestration targets to evolving bottlenecks.
paragraphs.zh: 许多智能体自我改进方法只优化单一预定义组件。 STaR（Zelikman 等，2022）通过对自生成且能得出正确答案的推理过程反复微调来改进模型参数。 AFlow（Zhang 等，2025）搜索以代码表示的工作流，而递归框架自我改进（Lee 等，2026）则利用修订历史上的成对反馈来改进提示层级的框架规格。 相关方法包括用于语言模型流水线优化的 DSPy（Khattab 等，2024）、用于反思式提示演化的 GEPA（Agrawal 等，2026），以及在智能体程序上进行元智能体引导搜索的 ADAS（Hu 等，2025）。 与之相比，AlphaEvolve（Novikov 等，2025）通过基于执行的评估来演化候选程序，其目标是任务产物而非智能体的改进流程。 Self-Refine（Madaan 等，2023）利用自我反馈迭代地修订输出，Reflexion（Shinn 等，2023）保留言语反思以指导后续尝试，而 Voyager（Wang 等，2024）则积累可复用的可执行技能。 Co-Harness（Chen 等，2026d）和 HarnessForge（Chen 等，2026b）通过交替进行框架改进与模型优化，将外部结构与内部能力联系起来。 它们的耦合更新解决了模型与框架的兼容性问题，但规定的更新顺序使得如何让工作流编排目标适应不断变化的瓶颈仍未得到解决。

sents.en: AFlow ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) searches code-represented workflows, while Recursive Harness Self-Improvement ( Lee et al., 2026 ) refines prompt-level harness specifications using pairwise feedback over revision histories.
sents.zh: AFlow（Zhang 等，2025）搜索以代码表示的工作流，而递归框架自我改进（Lee 等，2026）则利用修订历史上的成对反馈来改进提示层级的框架规格。

sents.en: Related approaches include DSPy ( Khattab et al., 2024 ) for language-model pipeline optimization, GEPA ( Agrawal et al., 2026 ) for reflective prompt evolution, and ADAS ( Hu et al., 2025 ) for meta-agent-guided search over agent programs.
sents.zh: 相关方法包括用于语言模型流水线优化的 DSPy（Khattab 等，2024）、用于反思式提示演化的 GEPA（Agrawal 等，2026），以及在智能体程序上进行元智能体引导搜索的 ADAS（Hu 等，2025）。

sents.en: In contrast, AlphaEvolve ( Novikov et al., 2025 ) evolves candidate programs through execution-based evaluation, targeting task artifacts rather than the agent’s improvement procedure.
sents.zh: 与之相比，AlphaEvolve（Novikov 等，2025）通过基于执行的评估来演化候选程序，其目标是任务产物而非智能体的改进流程。

sents.en: Self-Refine ( Madaan et al., 2023 ) iteratively revises outputs using self-feedback, while Reflexion ( Shinn et al., 2023 ) retains verbal reflections to guide subsequent attempts and Voyager ( Wang et al., 2024 ) accumulates reusable executable skills.
sents.zh: Self-Refine（Madaan 等，2023）利用自我反馈迭代地修订输出，Reflexion（Shinn 等，2023）保留言语反思以指导后续尝试，而 Voyager（Wang 等，2024）则积累可复用的可执行技能。

sents.en: Co-Harness ( Chen et al., 2026d ) and HarnessForge ( Chen et al., 2026b ) connect external structure and internal capability by alternating harness refinement with model optimization.
sents.zh: Co-Harness（Chen 等，2026d）和 HarnessForge（Chen 等，2026b）通过交替进行框架改进与模型优化，将外部结构与内部能力联系起来。

sents.en: Their coupled updates address model–harness compatibility, but the prescribed update order leaves open how to adapt workflow orchestration targets to evolving bottlenecks.
sents.zh: 它们的耦合更新解决了模型与框架的兼容性问题，但规定的更新顺序使得如何让工作流编排目标适应不断变化的瓶颈仍未得到解决。

paragraphs.en: Beyond prescribed alternation, SIA ( Hebbar et al., 2026 ) uses trajectory and performance feedback to choose between harness and weight updates, while its selection policy relies on a frozen language-model prior. HASE ( Luo et al., 2026 ) integrates task solving and harness editing into one action space and trains the policy with GRPO. A complementary direction makes the improver itself editable: Hyperagents ( Zhang et al., 2026c ) co-evolves task-agent and meta-agent programs and demonstrates transferable improvement strategies, whereas MetaSkill-Evolve ( Wang et al., 2026 ) recursively updates task skills and their improvement procedures on different timescales. Building on these complementary directions, RSIFlow couples bottleneck-aware workflow orchestration with feedback-driven Meta-Harness evolution.
paragraphs.zh: 除了固定的交替模式之外，SIA（Hebbar et al., 2026）利用轨迹与性能反馈在框架更新与权重更新之间做出选择，而其选择策略依赖一个冻结的语言模型先验。 HASE（Luo et al., 2026）将任务求解与框架编辑整合到同一动作空间中，并使用 GRPO 训练策略。 一个互补的方向是让改进者本身也可被编辑：Hyperagents（Zhang et al., 2026c）让任务智能体与元智能体程序共同演化，并展示了可迁移的改进策略；而 MetaSkill-Evolve（Wang et al., 2026）则在不同时间尺度上递归地更新任务技能及其改进流程。 在这些互补方向的基础上，RSIFlow 将瓶颈感知的工作流编排与反馈驱动的 Meta-Harness 演化相结合。

paragraphs.en: Tab. 1 compares RSIFlow against model-only, harness-only, and joint model–harness baselines on six agentic benchmarks and two backbone sizes, averaging +3.11% over the strongest per-metric baselines. RSIFlow leads in 11 of 12 benchmark–backbone settings across code generation, tool use, and search-QA. Its overall scores reach 51.21% with Qwen3-4B and 59.86% with Qwen3-8B, surpassing the strongest baseline by 6.06% and 3.86%, respectively. The largest gain occurs on HumanEval+, where RSIFlow improves pass@1 by 14.02% with Qwen3-4B. On MBPP+, pass@1 improves by an average of 3.91% across backbones. For tool use, RSIFlow achieves the highest BFCL-v3 scores with both backbones and the best ACEBench result with Qwen3-4B. On retrieval-intensive tasks, it improves F1 by an average of 5.20% on 2Wiki across backbones and by 6.38% on HotpotQA with Qwen3-8B.

paragraphs.en: Table 2 evaluates adaptive workflow orchestration and Meta-Agent evolution over five rounds. Compared with Vanilla, RSIFlow improves Code, Tool Use, and SearchQA by 19.04%, 3.92%, and 18.20% , respectively, increasing the three-domain average by 13.72 %. While fixed-component workflows exhibit domain-specific strengths, adaptive orchestration achieves the highest scores across all three domains, outperforming the fixed workflow by 4.13% - 8.81% on average. Overall, RSIFlow exceeds the average of all four ablated variants by 6.17 %. Disabling Meta-Agent evolution reduces average performance by 5.74 % , highlighting the importance of distilling historical feedback into reusable skills and principles. These results demonstrate that adaptive component orchestration enables balanced cross-domain improvements, while experience-driven Meta-Harness evolution further strengthens workflow effectiveness.

paragraphs.en: We evaluate RSIFlow with three Meta-Agent backbones over five evolution rounds on HumanEval+. As shown in Fig. 4 , all three models achieve overall performance improvements, with gains of 11.48%, 5.09%, and 24.41% for Claude-Sonnet-5, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and GPT-5.6-Sol, respectively. GPT-5.6-Sol achieves the highest final performance of 68.29%, albeit with greater API token consumption. From Round 3 to Round 5, it improves by 13.08%, compared with 6.15% and 4.17% for the other two backbones, suggesting that stronger Meta-Agents may better leverage accumulated intervention feedback. paragraphs.en: Fig. 5 illustrates five rounds (R1–R5) of RSIFlow evolution, following a Harness–Harness–Model–Model–Artifacts sequence. In R1, the Meta-Agent addresses output-format violations with an output-contract check (H1), reaching 32.23%. R2 builds on H1 to introduce receipt-grounded verification (H2) for unsupported completions, raising the score to 38.04%. To address persistent semantic errors, R3 shifts to Model optimization with 3,798 replay calls for LoRA fine-tuning, reaching 45.46% and distilling the model-specific skill M1. R4 reuses and supplements M1 with new evidence, expanding training to 5,397 calls and improving the score to 47.11%. In R5, execution feedback and accumulated repair guidance support code revision and resubmission within budget, reaching 51.21% while preserving the Model and Harness. Across these rounds, skills and general principles progressively refine the Meta-Agent’s bottleneck diagnosis and subsequent workflow orchestration. This lineage demonstrates how adaptive workflow orchestration and Meta-Harness evolution reinforce each other, yielding an overall improvement of 18.98%.

paragraphs.en: We presented RSIFlow , a recursive self-improvement framework coupling adaptive workflow orchestration with Meta-Agent evolution. Using accumulated execution feedback, the Meta-Agent identifies Task-Agent bottlenecks and selects Model, Harness, or Artifacts workflows. It distills successful and unsuccessful outcomes into reusable skills and principles to evolve its Meta-Harness. Across six benchmarks and two backbones, RSIFlow outperforms the strongest evaluated baseline in 11 of 12 settings. Ablations validate both mechanisms, while budget analyses show a favorable performance–budget trade-off. These results demonstrate that continual Meta-Agent evolution enhances system effectiveness alongside adaptive workflow orchestration.

paragraphs.en: RSIFlow is primarily evaluated using Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B as Task-Agent backbones. This setting is particularly relevant to resource-constrained agent deployments, where adaptive workflow orchestration enables targeted modifications to identified bottleneck components, while Meta-Agent evolution further improves bottleneck diagnosis and orchestration capabilities. However, whether these benefits remain significant with larger backbone models and at cluster scale remains unexplored. Future work will extend the evaluation to larger-scale settings to assess the scalability of RSIFlow.

paragraphs.en: RSIFlow couples the Task-Agent and Meta-Agent, evolving the Meta-Harness through reusable skills and general principles to improve workflow orchestration without updating the Meta-Agent’s model parameters. However, this process introduces additional computational overhead, while adopting a lower-cost Meta-Agent may compromise evolution gains. Moreover, the stability of experience-driven Meta-Harness updates remains to be fully investigated. Future work will explore counterfactual analysis to identify Meta-Agent deficiencies, apply targeted local modifications, and investigate Meta-Agent parameter optimization to improve evolution efficiency and stability.

paragraphs.en: We evaluate self-improvement across code generation, tool use, and multi-hop question answering. This section describes the six benchmarks, the update mechanisms of the baselines, and the experimental configurations. Appendix B gives the algorithms for the three intervention routes.

Our evolution pool contains 3,000 distinct training tasks, partitioned into five task-disjoint batches of 600 tasks each. Each round uses 200 code-generation tasks, 200 tool-use tasks, and 200 multi-hop questions. The fixed reporting set contains 744 tasks. Table 4 gives the dataset-level allocation.

TACO Li et al. (2023) contains algorithmic programming problems that require implementing a program from a natural-language specification and satisfying its input/output contract. We use 1,000 training problems from the TACO portion of the DeepCoder-Preview-Dataset . The selected tasks include standard-input/output and function-based interfaces, with correctness assessed by executing the submitted program against task-specific tests. They provide execution trajectories and feedback for improving program construction, interface handling, and algorithmic reasoning. The allocation contributes 200 tasks per evolution round; HumanEval+ and MBPP+ are reserved for reporting evaluation.

EnvScaler Song et al. (2026) provides executable, stateful environments in which agents solve tasks through sequences of tool calls. Each task specifies a user goal and an initial environment state; the agent must choose tools, construct arguments, and adapt its actions to returned observations. Task-specific validation checks assess whether the resulting state satisfies the goal. We allocate 1,000 scenarios to training, comprising 824 from the source dataset’s train split and 176 from its heldout split. Both source partitions are assigned to the training role in our study; tool-use reporting uses BFCL-v3 and ACEBench. Each evolution round contains 200 EnvScaler scenarios. Different training tasks may share an environment, so the round-disjoint allocation refers to task instances rather than environment families.

HotpotQA ( Yang et al., 2018 ) contains questions that require combining evidence across Wikipedia passages, including bridge and comparison questions. 2WikiMultiHopQA ( Ho et al., 2020 ) requires following multi-hop relations across entities and combining the retrieved facts into an answer. We select 500 questions from the official training split of each dataset. The Task-Agent retrieves evidence through the search interface and produces an answer, providing trajectories for improving evidence retrieval and multi-step reasoning. Each round uses 100 HotpotQA and 100 2WikiMultiHopQA training questions. Reporting uses a separate fixed set of 100 questions from each dataset’s official development split.

Code, tool use, and multi-hop QA each account for one third of the training pool, giving a domain ratio of 1 : 1 : 1 1{:}1{:}1 . Within QA, HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA have equal weight. The five training batches are fixed with split seed 42 and contain distinct task IDs. These counts describe the task allocation; candidate retries and reuse of eligible training trajectories do not create additional distinct tasks. Training and reporting use the separate source partitions described above, with overlap checks and feedback isolation specified in Appendix A.3 .
Counts refer to task instances rather than generated trajectories.

The reporting set contains 744 tasks: 342 code-generation tasks, 202 tool-use tasks, and 200 multi-hop questions. Each method is evaluated on the same task IDs with the same benchmark-specific scorer. Table 5 summarizes the task counts and reported metrics.

HumanEval+ asks the agent to implement a Python function from its signature and natural-language specification. Its 164 tasks test functional correctness, including edge cases exposed by the augmented EvalPlus tests ( Liu et al., 2023 ) . MBPP+ asks for short Python programs from natural-language descriptions and illustrative tests, covering basic algorithms, data structures, and program construction. We use a frozen 178-task subset of MBPP+ v0.2.0. For both benchmarks, a task succeeds when the final submitted program passes the base and augmented test suites. We report system pass@1: one final submission per task after the allowed agent execution. HumanEval+ uses v0.1.10, and both benchmarks use EvalPlus revision 26d6d00 with the recorded parser and process-isolation adapters.

BFCL-v3 evaluates function selection and argument construction in single-call, multiple-call, parallel-call, relevance, and multi-turn settings ( Patil et al., 2025 ) . These settings cover complementary aspects of tool use: selecting an appropriate function, supplying the required arguments, coordinating multiple calls, and determining whether an available tool is relevant to the request. The multi-turn tasks also test whether the agent maintains context across stateful tool interactions, connecting individual call decisions to the evolving interaction history. Our subset contains 152 tasks across 17 categories; native category-specific checks determine correctness, and the aggregate is weighted by the number of tasks. This weighting reflects the composition of the evaluated subset, with categories containing more tasks contributing proportionally more to the reported aggregate.

ACEBench evaluates API use under Normal, Special, and Agent settings, including ordinary function calls, incomplete or ambiguous instructions, and multi-step interactions ( Chen et al., 2025 ) . Together, these settings examine how agents translate user requests into API actions under different instruction and interaction conditions. We use 50 English tasks, which produce 57 native scoring records. We report the native weighted score and separately retain complete-task success; these quantities use different denominators. The distinction matters because one task can contribute more than one native scoring record. Record-level scoring describes the evaluator’s individual scoring units, whereas complete-task success summarizes outcomes at the original task level. We therefore specify both task and scoring-record counts when describing this evaluation.

HotpotQA requires combining evidence from multiple Wikipedia passages to answer bridge or comparison questions ( Yang et al., 2018 ) . We use 100 development questions with the v1 fullwiki protocol. 2WikiMultiHopQA requires composing facts about multiple entities along multi-hop reasoning chains ( Ho et al., 2020 ) ; we use 100 development questions and the original v1 evaluator. These tasks test whether agents can connect dispersed evidence and resolve questions requiring relational reasoning. For both benchmarks, the agent retrieves evidence through the search interface and submits an answer. The main metric is normalized answer-token F1, with exact match (EM) retained separately. The evaluator revisions are 3635853 for HotpotQA and 13800e5 for 2WikiMultiHopQA.

We separate training-time evolution from evaluation on the 744-task reporting set. For each evaluated evolution horizon n n , we first complete n n rounds on training tasks and then evaluate the resulting system on the reporting set. Reporting tasks are excluded from Task-model fine-tuning. Reporting-set scores and item-level evaluation feedback are never used for workflow selection, candidate acceptance, skill maintenance, Meta-Harness revision, or manual selection of system versions. Evaluations at different horizons measure the corresponding training-derived states; their results are not fed back into subsequent evolution.

The gain-based acceptance rule in the evolution algorithm applies only to training-time batches. The batch-level Artifacts procedure, including its two-attempt allowance and fallback to the parent, is not run on the reporting set. During reporting, the skill library and Meta-Harness remain fixed across tasks. Permitted environment feedback includes execution-interface signals such as context-length limit errors and output-length or format violations; it does not provide access to the reporting evaluator for optimization or output selection. Reference answers and hidden-test correctness signals are likewise excluded from generation and output selection. All compared methods receive the same environment feedback, tool permissions, and per-task execution budgets.

We additionally checked the frozen training and reporting manifests for overlap in task identifiers, recorded normalized prompt hashes, and recorded task-group identifiers, finding no matches between the two sets. This check establishes separation under these matching criteria; it does not assess semantic paraphrases or contamination in the backbone models’ pretraining data. Equal per-task execution budgets likewise do not imply equal total evolution cost.

We compare seven baselines using Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) . Within each backbone scale, the comparison protocol uses a common initial checkpoint and Task-Harness, task IDs, and evaluators. Table 6 summarizes editable Task components, weight training, Harness updates, adaptive component selection, and Meta-Agent evolution. These dimensions distinguish how each baseline allocates adaptation across model parameters, task components, and orchestration.

SFT trains on successful Task-Agent trajectories while keeping the Harness fixed. GRPO samples groups of trajectories, scores their task outcomes, and updates the model using group-relative rewards ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . Both methods improve the Task model without a component-selection mechanism.

AFlow searches executable agent workflows through iterative proposal and evaluation ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . MermaidFlow represents workflows as graphs and searches their structure ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) . These are the Harness-only configurations used in the main comparison. HarnessForge combines feedback-guided Harness modification with model training in a prescribed co-adaptation procedure ( Chen et al., 2026b ) . SIA uses execution feedback to choose between Harness and model updates ( Hebbar et al., 2026 ) .

HyperAgents makes both the Task-Agent and Meta-Agent programs editable, allowing the improvement procedure itself to evolve ( Zhang et al., 2026c ) . Its code-editing mechanism differs from parameter training. RSIFlow selects among Model, Harness, and Artifacts interventions and updates its Meta-Harness through accumulated intervention skills. The comparison therefore separates access to multiple Task-update routes from the ability to revise the Meta-Agent that chooses and implements them.

The main configuration uses Qwen3-4B or Qwen3-8B as the Task model and GPT-5.6 Sol as the Meta model. Each of the five evolution rounds permits at most two candidate attempts. Candidates share the same parent, training batch, and evaluator; the first valid candidate with positive paired gain is accepted. Meta model parameters remain fixed throughout evolution.

Table 8 lists the supplied 4B SFT/GRPO training settings. The separate comparison uses B1 for training and B2 for evaluation, as defined in Appendix C.1 ; its evaluation temperature does not specify decoding for all main experiments. These settings provide context for interpreting the reported SFT and GRPO results, with B1 and B2 serving distinct roles in the training and evaluation stages of this specific experimental comparison.

The loop has two coupled outputs: an accepted Task state and an updated improvement mechanism. Every candidate starts from the same round parent, so rejected edits do not accumulate. Failed implementation attempts and non-improving evaluations still enter the experience record. On a new task batch, task-bound outputs are generated anew; reusable knowledge is carried by the Meta-Harness and accepted changes to the Task model or Harness.

The Meta workflow connects six operations: evidence collection, diagnosis, skill retrieval, component intervention, paired evaluation, and skill integration. Diagnosis returns a bottleneck hypothesis with trajectory references; retrieval returns applicable procedures and counterexamples; intervention returns a candidate and its change record; evaluation returns paired outcomes; integration returns the next active skill set and the Action changes needed to use it.

A decision record binds the selected component to its expected behavioral effect and preservation constraints before construction. The Model branch receives eligible trajectories and a training configuration; the Harness branch receives a localized modification brief and interface contract; the Artifacts branch receives the Task’s own output and permitted feedback. Evaluation determines Task acceptance, while the entire record informs Meta evolution. An accepted Task change and a revised Meta procedure are thus separate decisions within the same loop.

The Model route updates the current model parameters while keeping the Task-Harness fixed and performing no direct Artifacts revision. Preserving Artifacts in this branch refers to the intervention scope; the candidate model generates its own outputs during evaluation. For example, a permitted test may expose an omitted empty-input branch. The Task-Agent inspects the failing path, adds the required branch, and resubmits. This illustrates the interface rather than an additional measured benchmark case. Hidden evaluator answers are never revision inputs. Stateful tool tasks require execution or replay against the registered environment state: editing a final textual claim cannot establish that an operation succeeded.

The Artifacts component in the main-text Task state denotes task-bound deliverables. Writing it as A t , x A_{t,x} makes the task index explicit: a revised output is retained for continued work on task x x , while a new task x ′ x^{\prime} produces its own A t , x ′ A_{t,x^{\prime}} . Cross-task reuse occurs through the Meta-Skill library 𝒦 t \mathcal{K}_{t} , which retains repair conditions, procedures, outcomes, and limitations. Meta retrieves this guidance to select and guide revision on a later task; the Task-Agent generates and revises that task’s own output. The R5 case is summarized in Appendix C.3 .

A Task-Harness skill implements reusable task-execution behavior, whereas a Meta-Skill guides diagnosis and intervention. Updating the former is a Harness intervention; distilling the latter is a subsequent Meta-level update. Persistent resource files or memory are therefore distinct from the task-bound output revised by the Artifacts route. Table 10 summarizes these boundaries.

Code: a permitted test reveals an omitted boundary case; Task-Agent edits the program, retests, and resubmits the source. Tool Use: an API reports a missing argument; the Task-Agent corrects and resubmits its structured call through the existing interface, with success established by the resulting environment receipt. SearchQA: retrieved evidence reveals an entity mismatch; the Task-Agent revises its answer using that evidence while keeping the retrieval Harness fixed. These examples illustrate the intervention scope, rather than additional measured cases.
We report the Model-update comparison, additional rollout-budget results, and two complementary views of Task–Meta evolution.

Table 8 gives the recorded 4B configurations. The two replay updates described in the main HHMMA case use 3,798 and 5,397 eligible calls. The separate SFT/GRPO comparison uses 2,780 eligible SFT calls from 1,200 source tasks, versus 6,000 GRPO trajectories from 3,000 tasks. GRPO carries the adapter and optimizer across five 600-task batches. The supplied optimization trace contains 100 optimizer updates; the trajectory count describes collection, while the trace describes recorded optimization steps.

Both methods start from the original Qwen3-4B checkpoint, train with the same B1 Harness, and report with the same B2 Harness. B1 denotes the complete-source/shape-check Harness, and B2 its receipt-check successor. These labels identify training and evaluation configurations in this separate SFT/GRPO comparison; its SFT-1200 and GRPO-3000 results are not the SFT and GRPO baseline rows in the main results table. SFT selects 2,780 calls from 300 successful tasks among 1,200 source tasks; GRPO samples two trajectories for each of 3,000 tasks. Both complete all 744 reporting tasks. GRPO reaches 368 complete-task successes versus 356 for SFT, a difference of 12 tasks or 1.61%. This complete-task success rate uses binary outcomes across 744 tasks and differs from the benchmark-score average reported as Overall in the main results. This comparison varies the training objective and data budget jointly.

Figure 6 complements the final results with training dynamics and data-collection cost. Panel (a) summarizes 100 optimizer steps across five rollout batches; the five-step statistics are computed within each batch and describe local loss fluctuations. Panel (b) shows higher GRPO scores on five benchmarks and an unchanged MBPP+ score. Complete-task success increases from 47.85% to 49.46%, while recorded rollout usage increases from 257.1M to at least 1,162.2M tokens. These totals count input and output tokens used to collect training trajectories, including the historical collection cost attributed to SFT; evaluation, Meta calls, and optimizer computation are excluded. SFT reuses trajectories from 1,200 source tasks without new sampling, whereas GRPO collects two trajectories per task from 3,000 tasks. Complete-task success increases by 1.61%, accompanied by substantially greater trajectory collection costs. The two configurations therefore illustrate different performance–collection cost trade-offs within the Model intervention route.

Figure 7 provides an additional view of the rollout-budget trade-offs on ACEBench, HotpotQA, and BFCL-v3. The horizontal axis measures rollout count, and the vertical axis reports each benchmark’s score. The empirical Pareto boundary identifies configurations for which no evaluated alternative achieves an equal or higher score with an equal or smaller rollout budget and a strict improvement in at least one dimension. RSIFlow attains the highest observed score on all three benchmarks, with several configurations lying on the empirical Pareto boundary. The budget response differs across tasks: BFCL-v3 scores level off at larger budgets, ACEBench improves further toward the largest RSIFlow budget, and HotpotQA exhibits intermediate fluctuations before reaching its highest score. Together with the main-text results, these observations show that the benefit of additional rollouts is benchmark-dependent and motivate allocating improvement effort according to the current task response.

The main-text case follows Harness–Harness–Model–Model–Artifacts (HHMMA). Table 9 links each reported average to the intervention and the knowledge available for the next round. Figure 8 presents the same sequence. Meta 0 acts in R1 and Meta 4 in R5; each intervention’s feedback updates the Meta version used next.

R1 addresses output-format violations by introducing the output-contract check H1, achieving an average score of 32.23%. R2 reuses H1 and prior experience to address unsupported completions through receipt-grounded verification H2, increasing the score to 38.04%. The two rounds apply a shared contract-checking criterion to different execution defects: submitting the required deliverable and verifying that a claimed operation succeeded.

As semantic errors persist, R3 shifts to Model optimization. R3 introduces M1 through 3,798 replay calls; R4 reuses that procedure with 5,397 calls. The second application supplements M1 rather than creating a duplicate skill. The reported scores are 45.46 and 47.11.

Finally, R5 shifts to Artifacts refinement. The Task-Agent uses execution feedback and prior repair guidance to edit, test, and resubmit its current code within budget, keeping the Model and Harness fixed. This targets a local output defect without an additional model-training or Harness-reconstruction step. The final reported average is 51.21%, 18.98% above R1. This measures the span from the first reported intervention to the fifth. Reusable repair guidance enters Meta-Skills; the revised code remains specific to the current task.

The main text also reports a different comparison: Meta versions modify a common initial Task-Agent rather than successively inheriting the Task states of the HHMMA case. Table 12 reproduces the reported domain scores. Its intervention labels are H–H–M–A–H because they belong to this separate comparison, not to the five-round HHMMA trajectory.

Meta0 and Meta4 both select Harness changes, yet their reported Code scores differ by 20.56% and their QA scores by 9.51%. Selecting the same component therefore does not determine the quality of the proposed modification. Meta3 has the highest reported Tool Use score in this table, showing that the ordering of Meta versions is domain-dependent. Across the selected versions, Code and QA show larger score variation than Tool Use, indicating that the observed performance differences between Meta versions are more pronounced in some domains than others. The sequential case tracks evolving Task states; the common-initialization comparison evaluates different Meta versions on the same Task parent.

Figure 9 complements the main-text sensitivity analysis with a cumulative-token view. From Round 1 to Round 5, HumanEval+ pass rates increase from 42.12% to 53.60% for Claude-Sonnet-5, from 44.42% to 49.51% for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and from 43.88% to 68.29% for GPT-5.6-Sol, corresponding to gains of 11.48%, 5.09%, and 24.41%. Their final cumulative Meta-Agent token counts are 177.7M, 211.2M, and 252.6M, respectively. GPT-5.6-Sol reaches 60.13% after four rounds using 91.8M tokens; its fifth round consumes an additional 160.8M tokens for a further 8.16% improvement. Claude-Sonnet-5 achieves a higher final pass rate than DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with fewer cumulative tokens, while DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash exhibits a small third-round decline. These trajectories illustrate how the observed performance–token trade-off varies across Meta-Agent backbones and evolution rounds.

A general principle abstracts a shared decision criterion from component-specific cases. For example, completion requiring task-appropriate evidence connects a source-code contract check with a tool-receipt check, while their implementations remain separate. The abstraction records source cases and applicability conditions; reuse contributes another response record rather than automatically expanding its scope.

The cards in Appendix F.3 present three component-specific procedures and one general selection principle. The Harness and Model cards summarize stored procedures and their observed feedback. The Artifacts card formulates feedback-guided revision of the Task-Agent’s own output under a limited budget. The final card synthesizes how failure scope and intervention cost guide component selection.

Applicability conditions determine when a procedure can be reused. On a new task, Meta retrieves relevant revision guidance and uses it to guide the Task-Agent in revising that task’s own output from its feedback. The Artifacts procedure and general principle express methodological guidance rather than additional measured intervention outcomes.

The submission-contract skill applies when the required deliverable is source code but the agent returns prose or execution output. Its reusable content is the condition under which a complete-source check should be invoked and the execution behavior that enforces it. Reuse therefore changes how subsequent tasks are handled by the Harness. A valid submission can still contain an algorithmic error, so satisfying the output contract resolves an interface failure without establishing semantic correctness. This distinction explains why later feedback can motivate a different intervention route.

The replay skill describes how verified successful Task-Agent calls become training examples. Checkpoint provenance, task identity, native success, and target validity determine whether a call provides suitable evidence for the update. Reusing this skill means applying the same data-selection and training procedure to the current parent and available trajectories. R4 supplements M1 because it provides another observed response to that procedure. The added evidence informs when replay is useful; it does not imply that increasing replay volume always improves every task domain.

The output-revision skill targets a defect that permitted feedback localizes within the Task-Agent’s current submission. Its steps operate through the existing interface: inspect the feedback, edit the relevant output, test the revision, and resubmit within budget. The reusable element is this conditional repair procedure, including the circumstances in which further retries are unlikely to help. A later task supplies its own program or answer and its own feedback. Thus, the skill can guide a new revision without transferring the earlier answer or changing the Task-Harness.

A general principle connects these procedures through a shared decision criterion. The same failed coding task may require a submission check, learning from successful trajectories, or a local program edit. The relevant distinction is where the failure occurs and which available intervention can address it under the remaining budget. A bounded output repair is appropriate when the feedback identifies an actionable defect; a recurring execution problem motivates a Harness change, while a persistent capability gap with eligible training data motivates a Model update. The principle guides this comparison while component-specific skills supply the concrete procedure.

Let 𝒮 t \mathcal{S}_{t} and 𝒫 t \mathcal{P}_{t} denote the component-specific skills and general principles distilled from e t e_{t} . Maintained skills replace the previous active Skill content. Meta then revises the Action interfaces, retrieval calls, stage-specific instructions, and supplementary prompts that consume those skills:

For example, a receipt-verification skill informs which evidence diagnosis requests, which checks the Harness branch generates, and which counterexamples evaluation inspects. Updating a record and updating its invocation flow are recorded separately. The result is a changed Meta-Harness, not just a larger collection of text.

HHMMA illustrates knowledge development: H1 supplies a contract-checking criterion for H2 at R2; M1 accumulates training response evidence at R4; and R5 formulates a bounded output-repair procedure for local code defects. R2-to-R3 shifts from execution checks to Model updates when semantic errors persist. The case illustrates reuse within an evolving system; it does not isolate the causal contribution of an individual skill.

Retrieval provides Meta with a procedure; integration guides its use in the next attempt. Applicability informs diagnosis, procedures inform modification briefs, and preservation requirements constrain construction and validation. For example, a receipt-grounded skill links an unsupported completion claim to the evidence needed for assessment. The Harness change implements this check; paired evaluation determines whether it improves task outcomes. This chain connects the stored lesson to an intervention whose effects can be examined.

Intervention responses inform library maintenance. Improvements support procedures under observed conditions; regressions reveal preservation failures. Failed candidates can inform diagnosis even when the parent Task state is retained. Supplementation adds evidence; revision updates inappropriate guidance. Task acceptance and Meta learning thus respond differently, while lessons remain linked to their source cases.

Recent work on LLM agents explores approaches to adapting execution structures, maintaining persistent memory, and coordinating information acquisition. HarnessForge ( Chen et al., 2026b ) jointly evolves execution harnesses and reasoning policies through failure-guided harness modification and harness-conditioned policy alignment. For persistent memory, All-Mem ( Lv et al., 2026a ) separates online retrieval from offline topology consolidation, preserving evidence while supporting retrieval under bounded computational budgets. Typed links enable budgeted expansion from anchors to archived evidence. For breadth-oriented information gathering, moreover, A-MapReduce ( Chen et al., 2026c ) decomposes wide-search objectives into parallel retrieval tasks and aggregates results, using experiential memory to refine task allocation and recomposition. These approaches improve how agents organize execution and retain or acquire information, with emphases on system compatibility, memory maintenance, and scalability.

A complementary line of research studies the structure and granularity of supervision for agent learning and language model post-training. GEAR ( Lv et al., 2026b ) models prerequisite and activation dependencies among rubric criteria with a probabilistic graphical framework, suppressing unsupported criterion contributions when constructing scalar rewards. The resulting reward captures criterion dependencies at the response level. For long-horizon agent distillation, AlignOPSD ( Chen et al., 2026a ) aligns privileged supervision with functionally corresponding decisions and distributes outcome-based credit across variable-duration decision spans and their constituent turns. TRCA ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) derives step-level supervision from action-induced state transitions using Evidence, Execution, and Invalidity rubrics. Its foundational reward evaluates local transition quality, while its breakthrough reward recognizes newly satisfied task conditions, providing fine-grained learning signals without requiring successful reference trajectories or learned process evaluators, even when terminal success feedback is sparse.
